claims.text: A mixed economic system is an economic system in which resources are allocated partly by market forces acting through prices and private firms, and partly by government through its budget, its public services and the firms it owns.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A market economic system leaves allocation to private owners responding to prices, a command system places allocation with a central authority, and a mixed system combines elements of the two, with the balance drawn differently in different countries.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: In a mixed economic system the private sector tends to produce everyday goods and services for markets, while government provides state services such as schools and hospitals, builds infrastructure, owns a share of firms and steps in where it judges a market outcome to be failing.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Namibia and Germany both run mixed economies: private firms trade through markets in each, while the state funds schools and hospitals, runs railways and sets rules, with the weighting between market and state differing between the two countries.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Government intervention to address market failure is deliberate action by a government to change the outcome a market reaches on its own, taken because the outcome is judged to waste resources or to leave needs unmet.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A maximum price held below the market price tends to make the quantity demanded exceed the quantity supplied, creating a shortage, while a minimum price held above the market price tends to make the quantity supplied exceed the quantity demanded, creating a surplus.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: An indirect tax raises the cost of supplying a good, which tends to raise its market price and reduce the quantity traded, while a subsidy lowers the cost of supplying a good, which tends to reduce its market price and raise the quantity traded.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A government can also intervene through regulation, which sets binding rules producers must follow; direct provision, in which the government supplies the good itself; privatisation, which moves a state-owned firm into private hands; and nationalisation, which moves a private firm into state ownership.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: On a demand and supply diagram a binding maximum price is a horizontal line below the equilibrium price; neither curve moves, the quantity demanded is read off the demand curve and the quantity supplied off the supply curve at that price, and the gap between them is the shortage, which tends to bring queues, rationing and black markets.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: On a demand and supply diagram a minimum price is a horizontal line above the equilibrium price; the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded at that price, the gap is the surplus, producers who sell receive more and consumers pay more and buy less, and the surplus may be bought and stored by the government at public cost.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: In the labour market the price is the wage rate: a minimum wage set above the market wage raises pay for workers who keep their jobs, contracts the quantity of labour demanded and extends the quantity supplied, leaving an excess supply of labour, which is unemployment; the more elastic demand for labour is, the larger the job losses, and a minimum wage set at or below the market wage has no effect.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A maximum wage set below the market wage holds pay down, so employers want more workers than offer themselves at that wage, leaving a shortage of labour and unfilled posts.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: In the foreign exchange market the price is the exchange rate: a minimum exchange rate held above the market rate leaves more of the currency offered than wanted, so the central bank buys the excess with its foreign currency reserves while they last; a maximum exchange rate held below the market rate leaves more wanted than offered, so the central bank sells its own currency and adds to its reserves.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: From 2011 to 2015 the Swiss central bank held a ceiling on the value of the Swiss franc against the euro, selling francs to stop it rising; the Namibian dollar is held at one-for-one with the South African rand, a fixed rate the Bank of Namibia backs with foreign currency reserves.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A subsidy paid to producers for each unit supplied lowers their costs, so the supply curve shifts down and to the right by the subsidy per unit while demand does not move; the new equilibrium has a lower price and a larger quantity, the price tends to fall by less than the subsidy, and the cost to the government is the subsidy per unit times the new quantity.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Maize meal sells at N$100 a 10 kg bag with 20 000 bags a week; a subsidy of N$5 a bag moves the equilibrium to N$97 and 21 500 bags, so buyers pay N$3 less, millers receive N$97 + N$5 = N$102 a bag, and the government pays N$5 x 21 500 = N$107 500 a week.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Regulation can cut harm or raise quality without the government buying anything, but complying adds to firms' costs, which may pass into prices, and a rule tends to work as well as it is inspected and enforced, which costs the government money.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Privatisation can push a firm to cut waste and improve service through the profit motive and, where rivals exist, competition, and it raises revenue for the government from the sale; but a private owner may raise prices, close loss-making services or shed workers, and a privatised firm with no rival may abuse its power unless it is regulated.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Nationalisation lets the state run a firm for social aims, such as keeping an essential service running, holding prices within reach and protecting jobs, but buying and running it costs public money, and without the profit motive or competition a state firm may be run less efficiently, with its losses covered by taxpayers.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Direct provision, in which the government supplies a good itself free or below cost, raises consumption of merit goods, supplies public goods and reaches households who cannot pay, but it is funded by taxes and other spending given up, and where demand outruns funding it may bring queues and lower quality.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Government failure occurs when an intervention leaves the allocation of resources worse than before, through poor information, side-effects such as shortages, black markets or stored surpluses, the cost of enforcement, or decisions shaped by political pressure; whether intervention works depends on how well the measure fits the failure, the information behind it, and whether its cost is smaller than the gain.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
